The Rufous hummingbird (Selasphorus rufus) begins life as a minuscule altricial nestling. Within the first few days after hatching, the body mass of a newly emerged chick is remarkably low, typically recorded at just 0.56 grams [Ww0 = 0.56 grams]. This nominal weight marks the starting point for an extraordinarily rapid growth phase that is energetically demanding. Despite this diminutive beginning, the rate of development is swift, with the hatching event itself occurring after an incubation period of approximately 16 days [ab = approximately 16 days] at a constant nest temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. The thermal environment of the nest is carefully regulated by the attending female to ensure proper embryonic development. The difference between this reported incubation duration at a controlled laboratory temperature and the slightly shorter 12 to 14 day periods often cited in field guides for wild nests suggests that ambient thermal variability in natural settings may accelerate embryonic growth rates, while the experimentally controlled 36 °C [T = 36 °C] condition results in a marginally extended developmental timeline.

As the nestling progresses, it undergoes a dramatic transformation from a nearly naked hatchling to a fully feathered juvenile. A critical milestone in this developmental trajectory is the achievement of fledging, which occurs 20 days after hatching [tx = 20 days after hatching] when maintained under the species' typical active metabolic temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This period is characterized by intense parental provisioning as the chick must more than sextuple its initial body mass to reach a functional size capable of flight. The adult body mass that females ultimately attain averages 3.6 grams [Wwi = 3.6 grams], a value that reflects the energetic constraints of a nectarivorous and insectivorous diet combined with the demands of egg production and incubation. Males, by contrast, tend to be slightly smaller, reaching an ultimate wet weight of approximately 3.3 grams [Wwi = approximately 3.3 grams], a sexual size dimorphism that is common among hummingbirds and is often linked to differences in aerial display behavior and territorial defense rather than substantial divergence in foraging ecology.

The transition from juvenile to a reproductively competent adult is governed by a cascade of hormonal and environmental cues. Under consistent thermal conditions typical of the breeding grounds, where body temperatures are sustained near 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] during active periods, puberty is attained at 150 days after hatching [tp = 150 days after hatching]. This delay between fledging and reproductive maturation allows young birds to refine their foraging skills, establish dominance hierarchies along migratory routes, and accumulate sufficient fat reserves for their first northward migration. The age at first reproduction, marking the initiation of a nesting attempt, is deferred considerably further, with the first brood being initiated at exactly 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], coinciding with the return to the breeding territories in the spring of their second calendar year at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This life-history scheduling represents a significant investment in survival during the first full annual cycle, which includes two demanding transcontinental migrations.

Reproductive output in this species is constrained by the high energetic costs of hovering flight and the brevity of the breeding season at northern latitudes. Females typically produce 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = 1 clutch per year], and each nesting attempt contains two eggs that are laid on consecutive days, yielding an annual reproductive output of 2 eggs [N_R_i = 2 eggs] per year. This modest annual fecundity is compensated by the high survival rates of adult females, which often return to the same breeding sites across multiple seasons. At the thermally neutral and metabolically active temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], the maximum daily reproductive rate is derived from these natural units rather than expressed as a numeric per-day value, reflecting the biological reality that female hummingbirds are income breeders who must balance daily nectar intake against the substantial protein demands of egg synthesis. The incubation and chick-rearing duties fall entirely on the female, further limiting the potential for multiple successful broods within a single summer.

Longevity records for this species indicate a remarkably long lifespan for such a small endotherm. The maximum documented lifespan, calculated from banding returns and reported as approximately 3,249 days [am = approximately 3,249 days] when measured at the typical active body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], is extraordinary compared to other passerine-sized birds and even some larger temperate passerines, reflecting the hummingbird's unique combination of a torpor-capable metabolism that conserves energy overnight and a low extrinsic mortality rate once adulthood is reached. The energetic costs of hovering flight may actually select for robust physiological maintenance pathways, as any reduction in cardiovascular or mitochondrial function would be immediately fatal during foraging. Thus, the life history of the Rufous hummingbird encapsulates a paradox: a minute hatchling that scales to a body mass of just a few grams, yet achieves a total lifespan measured in years rather than months, underscoring the evolutionary success of the trochilid bauplan in exploiting high-quality but temporally patchy floral resources across vast geographic ranges.
